idiom_name: Rule-of-Five RAII class forwarding to the C API
implementation_notes: The classic structure collapses into one local idiom: a class with a constructor that acquires the C resource, a destructor that releases it, deleted copy operations and a move constructor, plus inline methods that forward directly to the C functions and translate error codes. C++11 is the floor because deleted functions and move semantics are what make single ownership expressible. Keep the wrapper header-only or nearly so, and prefer this form only when no standard-library type already covers the resource.
pitfalls: A destructor that can throw or that ignores close() errors makes failure handling unpredictable; release in the destructor, report through an explicit close()/sync path.
Forgetting to delete the copy operations gives two owners for one descriptor and a double close; move semantics are what make the ownership single.
A wrapper method that returns the raw fd as the primary interface lets callers outlive the object and reuse a closed descriptor.

variants.name: Standard-library facades instead of hand-written wrappers
variants.implementation_notes: Before writing a wrapper, check the standard library: std::mutex, std::thread and std::condition_variable wrap the platform synchronization and threading APIs, std::fstream and std::filesystem wrap C stdio and the POSIX/Win32 directory calls, and std::scoped_lock/unique_lock own the locking discipline. These types forward to the same C APIs a hand-written facade would call, with the same (usually inlined) cost, and they are the ones the rest of the ecosystem expects. C++17 is the floor because the filesystem library and std::scoped_lock arrive there.
pitfalls: The standard wrappers cover the platform APIs but not a third-party C library: do not stretch std::fstream or std::thread to wrap something they never owned.
std::fstream and std::filesystem hide errors behind stream state and error_code overloads; a facade built on them must still surface the failure at the boundary.
Locking the same mutex through std::scoped_lock inside a callback re-entered from the wrapped C API deadlocks; the non-recursive default is deliberate.

variants.name: Opaque-handle (pimpl) facade for a stable binary boundary
variants.implementation_notes: When the facade is shipped as a library, the compiled structure is the design: declare the class with an incomplete Impl and a unique_ptr, define the destructor out of line in the implementation file, and keep all platform- and library-specific calls there. Clients see only the class and never recompile when the implementation, the platform branch or even the size of the state changes. This is the C++ form of the opaque handle used in C and the safe-handle form used in managed runtimes.
pitfalls: Without the out-of-line destructor the incomplete type fails to compile, and with a defaulted one the unique_ptr delete lands in the wrong translation unit.
Pimpl adds an allocation and a pointer indirection per call site that forwards through it; for a hot, tiny wrapper prefer the direct RAII class.
The stable boundary freezes the ABI but not the semantics: an implementation that changes error conventions still breaks callers.
